name: Circadian Architectural Regulation via Non-Visual Photoreception
short_description: Building design mediates ipRGC → SCN pathway; appropriate light timing produces circadian alignment, inappropriate light causes temporal PE and allostatic load
structural_pattern: Building design determines the spectral power distribution, intensity, timing, duration, and spatial distribution of light reaching the occupant's eyes. This light is transduced by melanopsin-expressing intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs), which project via the retinohypothalamic tract to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN). The SCN, as the master circadian pacemaker, generates temporal predictions (a ~24h oscillation) and uses the light signal to entrain this oscillation to the environmental day-night cycle. Appropriate light (high melanopic irradiance during the biological day, dim warm light during biological evening) produces small temporal PE and efficient circadian function. Inappropriate light produces temporal PE — misalignment between the SCN's predicted phase and the light signal — resulting in circadian disruption with cascading health, cognitive, and affective consequences via the allostatic pathway (T29).
higher_order_principle: Temporal prediction error at the circadian timescale. The SCN generates a 24-hour prediction; light calibrates it. Chronic mismatch = chronic temporal PE = allostatic load. This is the circadian instantiation of the same prediction-error-correction principle that operates at perceptual, attentional, and allostatic timescales.

causal_links.evidence_base: Window size, orientation, glazing transmittance, room depth, surface reflectance, electric lighting spectrum and intensity, and shading/control strategy jointly determine the melanopic irradiance at the occupant's cornea. Quantifiable via Circadian Stimulus (CS) metric or melanopic Equivalent Daylight Illuminance (mEDI) per CIE S 026.

Dose-response relationship characterized by Brainard et al. (2001). Nonlinear, with sigmoidal saturation. Dependent on wavelength (peak ~480nm), irradiance, duration, timing relative to circadian phase, and prior photic history.

ipRGC signal via retinohypothalamic tract to SCN. Phase response curve determines direction and magnitude of phase shift: morning light advances the clock; evening light delays it. (Khalsa et al., 2003, ~800 citations).

SCN → pineal (melatonin: onset ~2h before habitual bedtime, peak during sleep, suppressed by light). SCN → adrenal (cortisol: peak ~30min after waking, declining through day). Rhythm alignment = health; misalignment = disruption.

Aligned circadian function supports: sleep quality, daytime alertness, mood stability, metabolic health, immune function, cognitive performance. Misalignment impairs all of these. Chronic misalignment → allostatic load (T29).

scope_conditions: Applies to all occupied buildings — every building is a circadian instrument whether designed as one or not
Strongest effects for occupants with limited outdoor light exposure (deep-plan offices, healthcare, residential care, schools)
Timing effects are phase-dependent: same light has different circadian impact depending on when in the 24h cycle it is experienced
Individual differences in chronotype (morningness-eveningness) moderate the optimal timing of circadian light
moderators: Age: aging reduces ipRGC density and lens transmittance → elderly need more light for equivalent circadian stimulus
Chronotype: evening chronotypes are more vulnerable to insufficient morning light
Season and latitude: high-latitude winters provide insufficient daylight for circadian entrainment → architectural compensation needed
Building type: healthcare and shift-work environments have the most severe circadian challenges
Prior photic history: a dim morning reduces the circadian system's sensitivity to subsequent light

metrics.circadian_stimulus: CS ranges 0 to 0.7, effectiveness at activating circadian system
metrics.melanopic_EDI: mEDI per CIE S 026:2018, melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance

standard_dose_response.cs_threshold: CS ≥ 0.3 for ≥ 2 hours during morning/early afternoon

age_corrected_dose_response.medi_threshold: M-EDI ≥ 500 lux at eye level (approximately DOUBLE)
delivery_methods: Illuminated vertical surfaces at seated eye height
age_corrected_dose_response.design_implication: Standard ceiling-only overhead lighting is INSUFFICIENT for circadian needs in elderly populations

age_correction_function.precision: ±20% individual variation even within age cohorts
age_correction_function.mechanism: Progressive yellowing and thickening of crystalline lens attenuates short-wavelength light; by age 65, lens transmits ~50% of blue light compared to age 25

healthcare_design_implications: Senior living facilities need HIGHER melanopic irradiance than standard recommendations
Hospitals with elderly patients require enhanced circadian lighting
Buildings with aging workforce need circadian-optimized design
Light at eye level (task lights, illuminated vertical surfaces) more effective than overhead

interactions.nature: Circadian disruption is a major input to allostatic load. L2 specifies the light pathway; T29 specifies the downstream allostatic consequences.

L1 and L2 are independent pathways operating on the same physical stimulus (light). L1 = visual-aesthetic processing of luminance patterns. L2 = non-visual circadian processing of spectral irradiance.
Darkness functions as a threat signal (T5) AND as a circadian signal (L2). These are distinguishable: darkness at night is circadianly appropriate but may still trigger threat.
